content:
At the base of the Skytree there’s a dessert rooted in enmusubi traditions.

I think we can all agree that at any moment when you’re eating ice cream, you’re enjoying one of life’s great blessings. It’s when your dessert is finished that your mind will once again start to wonder about what your future fate will be, and to help answer that question, there’s Negawakuba.

Negaqakuba is a store in Solamachi, the entertainment complex at the base of the Skytree in Tokyo’s Oshiage neighborhood. It specializes in good-luck charms that draw on Shinto traditions and folklore, and that theme carries over to the attached cafe, which is offering Japanese-style ice cream parfaits with a side of fortune telling.

The Enmusubi no Goen Ice Manpuku no Imo is a special for-fall dessert with its most striking feature being the cookie styled like a bright red torii gate, of the kind that marks the entrance to Shinto shrine grounds. Forming a swirly cloud-like backdrop for the gate is a dollop of espuma cream, and providing the autumnal element are sweet potato chips, smooth sweet potato paste, and blocks of daigaku imo, glazed sweet potato sprinkled with black sesame. All of these sit atop a cup of salty vanilla ice cream.

The dessert is as packed with playful puns as it is mouthwatering ingredients. Enmusubi is a kind of good luck charm that’s said to help form good relationships, usually of the romantic kind, but also possibly for good business or general interpersonal connections. These happy relationships are called goen, but when written with different kanji characters, goen can also mean “honorable salt.” Likewise, the manpuku part of the Enmusubi no Goen Ice Manpuku no Imo’s name is written with the kanji for “10,000 blessings,” but in the context of food manpuku, if written differently, means “full/satisfied stomach.” With imo meaning either potato or sweet potato, you could translate Enmusubi no Goen Ice Manpuku no Imo as either “Filling Salty Ice Cream Sweet Potato Enmusubi” or “Blessed Good Relationship Seet Potato Enmusubi.”

By the way, if you’re wondering about that cute little bunny pictured next to the parfait in the above photo, that’s an usagi mikuji, a figurine shaped like a rabit (usagi) with a paper telling you your fortune (mikuji) inside. Usagi mikuji are sold at some Shinto shrines, and Negawakuba offers a set that bundles one with the Enmusubi no Goen Ice Manpuku no Imo for 1,275 yen (US$8). Alternatively, the dessert can be ordered a la carte for 750 yen, or with a cup of black tea grown in the town of Izumo, Shimane Prefecture, whose enmusubi are said to be especially effective.

Ah, but if you don’t order the set with the usagi mikuji, you won’t know you future, right? Not necessarily, because customers who order the parfait without the figurine are invited to draw their fortune from a traditional mikuji box…

…and also to ring a set of kagura suzu bells, used by shrine maidens during ceremonial dances, with a wish in their heart.

The parfait can be ordered as either an eat-in or to-go item. It’s on sale now, and will be offered while supplies last.

title: Go to hell! …at a limited time historical art exhibit coming to Osaka
description: It’ll be a hell of a good time. content:
It’ll be a hell of a good time.

The concept of hell has existed in Japan for a long time, but it’s a much more nebulous one compared to the clear-cut fire-and-brimstone version of Western countries. For example, saying things like “this job is hell” to a Japanese person is perfectly normal, but saying “it’s hot as hell” might come across a little weird as there is no immediate preconceived notion of hell being hot as opposed to also being cold, sharp, dark, urine-soaked, bloody… you get the idea.

Two versions of hell make up Japan’s overall view of it, the earliest being the Shinto concept of Yomi, which was more of a dark and foreboding place than a “hell” in the sense of people getting punished for their transgressions. But it still wasn’t really a nice place to be either, so it would be fair to call it a prototypical Japanese hell.

Later on, around the sixth century, Buddhism was introduced to Japan by way of China and Korea. By this time, China had really fleshed out an extremely intricate system of hells, with some counts in the tens of thousands and potentially an infinite amount beyond that, as each hell is tailored to an individual’s karmic infractions.

▼ One of the more comprehensive representations of Japanese hell can be seen in the Great Hell Painting (Dai-jigoku-e), a set of hanging scrolls kept in Chogaku Temple in the city of Tenri, Nara Prefecture.

Japanese Buddhism took these concepts and crafted an admittedly vague layout of this hell, also known as “Jigoku” to use the Buddhist terminology. It is so vague and convoluted that not many people in Japan really understand what it entails exactly. So to help with that, the Descent into Jigoku Exhibition Production Committee was assembled and created a traveling art exhibit to show how hell has been traditionally seen in Japan.

The exhibition takes guests through the process of death and the afterlife in order, starting with Kusozu (the nine stages of decay). The stages start with the last moments of life, then go through all the ideal metal band names such as “distention,” “exudation of blood,” and “putrefaction.” According to some historical texts, viewing these stages of decay either directly or through imagination can help one understand the impermanence of the physical form or resist urges of lust.

From there, you can visit Chu-u, also known as Bardo in Buddhism, which is a transitional space one goes to after death and before rebirth. Some schools say this is space in which you might encounter the Ten Kings of Jigoku who ruthlessly judge your mortal deeds and, in an almost comically bureaucratic fashion, assign you to the appropriate level of hell.

▼ Just another manic Monday at the office for the Ten Kings of hell.

One bright side to Buddhist hell is that it’s rarely eternal, unless you did something truly heinous. The purpose of hell here is to burn away your sins until your soul is pure enough to be reborn again. So don’t panic too much about that library book you returned late. You’ll only have to climb the Hell of the Mountain of Knives for one… two days tops.

The exhibition also shows you the Eight Great Hells, also known as the Eight Hot Hells as fire searing your flesh plays a big part in most of them. They involve a range of tortures from having animals devour your flesh and being repeatedly murdered to getting molten metal poured into your mouth and/or butt.

▼ This 13th-century work shows the bottom level of the Eight Great Hells. After death, one would fall for 2,000 years before reaching it, at which point they slam into that iron mesh and get diced up on impact. However, this being hell, they’re instantly regenerated and constantly seared by the unending fire as iron dogs and wardens with clubs relentlessly attack them. The wardens and dogs are a little hard to make out in all that fire, but you can see them at the bottom of the picture.

This would be the closest equivalent to a Western concept of hell, but many forms of Buddhism aren’t limited to just that. There’s also the Eight Cold Hells, which, as you can probably guess, involve freezing to death in a variety of ways, only to be instantly regenerated and forced to do it all over again. There are also a lot of sub-hells with more niche torture where dogs have fire for teeth, giant birds drop you from great heights, and chunks of iron rain from the skies.

▼ This work from the 12th century depicts the ancillary hell known as The Hell of Excrement, in which those who lived a spiritually corrupt life of greed must wade through a neck-deep pool of feces and urine while beset upon by giant maggots with needles for teeth.

The Descent into Jigoku exhibition presents these concepts using various works of art developed throughout Japan’s history. However, since some of these works have been deemed national treasures and important cultural properties, they are strictly regulated. Because of that, many pieces have been digitally recreated by the visual effects and spatial design wizards at KOO-KI using projection mapping and animation to make the wardens of hell literally leap off the page at you.

▼ “Better flip that person on the left! They’re a little overdone on that side.”

On the other hand, some real works will be present too, such as a statue of King Emna, one of the Ten Kings of Jigoku, owned by the exhibition’s supervisor and prominent expert in Japanese hell, Masahiko Tamura.

The exhibition’s next stop will be the Namba Parks Museum in Osaka from 28 November to 27 December. Admission is 2,800 yen ($18) for adults, 1,500 yen for students, and children under 3 get in for free, but I’m not sure how frequently or vividly the whole getting molten lead poured into the anus thing is depicted there, so parental discretion is advised.

title: New Transforming Business Card case brings anime mecha to Japanese work meetings
description: Mobile Suits and Mobile Stationery make meishi much more mecha. content:
Mobile Suits and Mobile Stationery make meishi much more mecha.

Exchanging business cards is serious business in Japan, with a whole series of steps and proper etiquette involved to ensure you make a good first impression. Called “Meishi Koukan” (“Business Card Exchange”), the first step in this dance involves keeping your cards in a business card holder (“meishi ire”) rather than loose in a pocket, and then, while standing, you must hold your card with both hands at chest-height, ensure the text faces the recipient, and if you’re in a lower-ranking position, you should hold your card lower than theirs as a sign of humility.

That’s a lot to remember, especially during a meeting, so wouldn’t it be nice if you had a gadget that could do all that work for you?

Well, as it turns out, Bandai Spirits has been on the case, quite literally, designing a business card case that automatically unfolds and presents your card perfectly, while lightening the mood with a bit of humour at the same time.

Called the Mobile Stationery Automatic Transforming Business Card Case, this is the first product in a new line of “Mobile Stationery” designed for young adults in the workplace, or “kidults” as Bandai likes to call them.

▼ Some of the promo images adopt the slightly clunky translation, “Automatic Transform Namecard Case”.

There are three new transforming business card cases coming our way, incorporating technology from the company’s Super Alloy line, which is known for its intricate mechanical designs and transforming gimmicks.

▼ The cases look like they’ve just rolled out of a Japanese mecha factory.

 

▼ The first model in the series is called “Toy Colour“.

The colour scheme evokes the look of the RX-78-2 Gundam, especially when loaded up with white business cards inside.

The two others could also likened to Gundam Mobile Suits, but Bandai refrains from making any connections, simply referring to them as Standard Colour…

▼ … and Black Colour.

The way it works is simple – add your business cards into the case, then hold the case towards your soon-to-be-awestruck business card recipient and press the button.

The inner mechanism rotates the card 180 degrees and pushes it forward upon opening, so it’s facing the person you’re greeting.

▼ This video shows the Mobile Stationery card case in action.

The dimensions of each case are approximately 12.5 x 9.5 x 2.5 centimetres (4.9 x 3.7 x 1 inches), and they’re designed to hold business cards that are 5.5 x 9.1 centimetres in size, with a recommended paper thickness of 0.24 millimetres.

Each case costs 3,300 yen (US$21) and is scheduled to be shipped out in October, with reservations being accepted through the brand’s online stores in Japan, Asia, the U.S. from 27 August (details here).

title: Studio Ghibli adds new finger puppets to its anime merchandise collection in Japan
description: The Robot Soldier and Fox Squirrel join Sheeta and Pazu in this beautiful Laputa: Castle in the Sky figurine collection. Just last month, Studio Ghibli wowed fans by releasing a huge collection of finger puppets, featuring characters from My Neighbour Totoro. Now, the studio is giving us another chance to wear our love for Ghibli […]
content:
The Robot Soldier and Fox Squirrel join Sheeta and Pazu in this beautiful Laputa: Castle in the Sky figurine collection.

Just last month, Studio Ghibli wowed fans by releasing a huge collection of finger puppets, featuring characters from My Neighbour Totoro. Now, the studio is giving us another chance to wear our love for Ghibli on our fingertips, this time with some of the cast from Laputa: Castle in the Sky.

▼ The puppets are made from soft vinyl, and while they’re designed to sit on your fingers, they also work well as beautiful figurines.

▼ The first finger puppet in the collection is Sheeta, the star of the movie who falls from the sky at the start of the film. 

This is a beautiful recreation of the main character, and it even features the mysterious blue crystal that she wears around her neck.

The pendant wields many powers, and it also helps to slow her descent when she falls from the sky, so she’s able to float gently into the arms of Pazu.

Pazu also joins Sheeta for this special release, with every detail of his working-class miner’s outfit faithfully recreated in miniature form.

His hat, vest, boots, gloves and aviator-style goggles make him instantly recognisable, while his wide-eyed expression captures the earnest, can-do attitude of his character.

The expression on Pazu’s face appears to change slightly depending on the angle, allowing you to bring extra emotional range to impromptu puppet scenes.

Rounding out the collection are two other essential members of the cast.

▼ The Robot Soldier

▼ And the Fox Squirrel.

The Robot Soldier does a remarkable job of expressing emotion throughout the movie, despite remaining silent the whole time. That combination of strength and sensitivity is beautifully reflected in this finger puppet.

▼ We can now give the robot all the love and attention it deserves.

▼ The Fox Squirrel also retains its mystique, while looking like it might spring to life at any time.

Together, the two characters have the power to save the world with love and cuteness, and they look so sweet together we don’t even mind how large the Fox Squirrel looks beside the Robot Soldier.

▼ The Fox Squirrel runs around the shoulders of the robot in the movie, looking much smaller than this puppet, but who are we to question what’s right or wrong in the Ghibli universe?

These puppets are a beautiful way to keep the magical world of Ghibli at your fingertips, and they can be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below) from 10 a.m. on 5 September, priced at 770 yen (US$4.93) each.

title: Kobe middle schools begin abolishing extracurricular activities, shift to community programs
description: The Kobekatsu program could end up being better for kids than the options they had before. Extracurricular activities are a big deal at schools in Japan, widely considered an important way for adolescents to develop a sense of responsibility and diligence while forging friendships, developing healthy fitness habits, and deepening their appreciation for the arts. […]
content:
The Kobekatsu program could end up being better for kids than the options they had before.

Extracurricular activities are a big deal at schools in Japan, widely considered an important way for adolescents to develop a sense of responsibility and diligence while forging friendships, developing healthy fitness habits, and deepening their appreciation for the arts. In some schools all students are actually required to join one of the school’s clubs or sports teams, and even at ones without such a rule, kids who don’t participate in any extracurricular activities, facetiously called members of the “going straight home” club, are decidedly in the minority.

However, as of September 1, many middle schools in Kobe have no extracurricular activities at all.

Extracurricular activities haven’t been temporarily suspendered at those schools due to damaged athletic fields, instructor sicknesses, or other temporary conditions. A total of 82 public middle schools have completely abolished their extracurricular programs, permanently disbanding their sports teams, marching bands, art clubs, and all other such groups.

▼ This could be a photo of one of the schools’ drama clubs.

The decision, recommended by the Kobe Board of Education, was prompted by two factors. Japanese public school teachers often find themselves stretched thin trying to prepare and teach lessons for their classes while also handling duties as instructors/coaches for extracurricular activities. With overwork being something that Japanese employers have become more sympathetic toward in recent years, if something has to give in a teacher’s schedule, it makes sense that the board would want them to prioritize their lessons.

Even if teachers have enough time to serve as advisors and coaches, though, with Japan’ s dwindlig birthrates, the clubs and teams don’t always have enough members. Even before abolishing their extracurricular programs entirely, some of the schools had already had to indefinitely disband certain teams and clubs as the number of students joining them was too small to keep them viable.

The good news is that the closing down of the schools’ extracurricular programs is also opening up new opportunities for the affected students. September 1 was also the start of a new program called Kobekatsu, katsu being a shortened form of bukatsu (“extracurricular activities”). Under the Kobekatsu program, the Kobe board of education has partnered with 1,051 local community sports teams, clubs, workshops, and universities that offer programs in athletics, the arts, and technology. Students at the schools which no longer offer extracurricular activities may join any of the Kobekatsu partner programs, and they receive a stipend of between 1,500 and 3,000 yen (US$9.50-US$19) a month to help cover participation costs, which average 3,200 yen per month. There’s also a fund being set up to help with the costs of procuring necessary equipment, such as sports supplies and musical instruments.

The shift to community and privately-run programs has the potential to diminish students’ sense of school pride, as even if students have classmates in their Kobekatsu club, the club is no longer representing the school. However, there are several potential upsides, with the increased choice provided to students being the most obvious. With over 1,000 partner organizations, students will have access to activities far beyond the range that their school could offer on its own.

Sure, there’s bound to be some overlap within the available activities, but even that’s something that could work out in students’ favor. It’s not unusual for kids to have an interest snuffed out by a short-tempered coach or unfriendly teammates, causing them to resent and even hate something they might have otherwise developed a lifelong passion for. With school-run clubs, you’re stuck with those personalities; if you’re playing baseball, and the coach is a jerk, then you’re going to be playing baseball with a jerk. On the other hand, Kobekatsu definitely has more than one baseball team among its 1,051 partners, and having more than one such group to choose from gives kids more options in finding a program with the atmosphere and culture that best nurtures their interest and talents.

In addition, since Kobekatsu activity choices aren’t restricted by address in the way that public middle school enrollment is, the new program will give participants an opportunity they wouldn’t otherwise have to interact with students from other schools, hopefully helping them become more open-minded, well-rounded individuals. So while it will be sad to see the schools’ clubs come to an end, this could be the start of something very good in its own right.

title: 7-Eleven Japan releases new Tsukimi Moon-Viewing range for autumn, with a must-try daifuku and teriyaki burger
description: Japanese convenience store chain brings the moon and rabbits to a new range of food for a limited time.  If you’re in Japan this month, you’re in for an absolute treat as 7-Eleven is releasing a limited-edition range of treats to celebrate the upcoming Moon-Viewing festival, known as “Otsukimi” or “Tsukimi” in Japanese. With Tsukimi […]
content:
Japanese convenience store chain brings the moon and rabbits to a new range of food for a limited time. 

If you’re in Japan this month, you’re in for an absolute treat as 7-Eleven is releasing a limited-edition range of treats to celebrate the upcoming Moon-Viewing festival, known as “Otsukimi” or “Tsukimi” in Japanese. With Tsukimi being celebrated on 25 September this year, 7-Eleven is giving us plenty of time to celebrate, as the new collection is being released across the country from 1 September.

The products will be easy to spot in stores, as they’re beautifully adorned with bunnies pounding rice, a nod to the Japanese belief that the markings on the moon resemble a rabbit pounding rice, and round, moon-esque ingredients like dumplings and egg feature heavily in the range.

▼ Let’s take a closer look at everything in the collection, starting with the Otsukimi Pudding Crepe (270 yen [US$1.69]), which is available from 1 September.

This soft, chewy crepe is wrapped around a smooth, custardy pudding made with egg and vanilla, and accompanied by a layer of creamy milk filling for an extra-soft mouthfeel and rich flavour.

▼ Otsukimi Roll Cake (270 yen), available from 1 September.

The classic Swiss roll gets a full-moon makeover with a generous swirl of smooth custard whipped cream inside a fluffy sponge. The presentation is simple yet striking, as the round shape is a delicious representation of the moon.

▼ Otsukimi Zenzai (346 yen), available from 15 September

As a traditional dessert, zenzai commonly contains sweetened adzuki beans, served with mochi or small, round shiratama rice dumplings. At 7-Eleven, the dessert has been transformed into a little moonlit scene, with sweet red bean paste representing the night sky, white whipped cream representing clouds and yellow shiratama rice dumplings resembling the moon.

▼ Big Moon Daifuku Custard Whip (300 yen), available from 15 September

Daifuku is a popular Japanese sweet made from soft, chewy mochi rice dough wrapped around a sweet filling. This moon-viewing version takes things to the next level in terms of size, as it’s around 8 centimetres (3.15 inches) in diameter, making it much bigger than traditional daifuku. Inside is a combination of rich custard and soft whipped cream, creating a great contrast between soft and chewy textures.

▼ Otsukimi Teriyaki Burger (378 yen), available from 9 September

Finally, we have the one savoury item in the range, which also looks set to become one of the most sought-after. Tsukimi Burgers have become popular limited-time menu items at fast food joints like McDonald’s and KFC in Japan, but they’re not a common sight at convenience stores, making this a very unique offering. The 7-Eleven Tsukimi Burger contains the salty sweet flavour of teriyaki sauce, and a fried egg designed to look like the full moon.

With careful thought given to the look and taste of each item in the collection, we can’t wait to try the entire range when all the products are in stores from 15 September. Until then, we’ll be munching on the chain’s viral flat criossants, which, when you think about it, also kind of look like the moon.

title: Join Naked in the Niwa garden: Kyoto Station’s newest spot to craft traditional art
description: Workshops offer English instruction in making custom gold leaf bags, weaving bamboo baskets, and crafting samurai armor. Many tourists descend upon the historical capital of Japan each day to appreciate its architectural beauty and cultural charm, but there are fewer who come away from their trip with a tangible traditional souvenir crafted by their own […]
content:
Workshops offer English instruction in making custom gold leaf bags, weaving bamboo baskets, and crafting samurai armor.

Many tourists descend upon the historical capital of Japan each day to appreciate its architectural beauty and cultural charm, but there are fewer who come away from their trip with a tangible traditional souvenir crafted by their own hand. Creative digital arts company Naked is launching interactive cultural workshops starting September 8, held every Tuesday and Thursday at Kyoto Station, that will give you a hands-on experience of a traditional craft.

Naked is a renowned Tokyo-based creative studio famous for blending projection mapping and digital art with historical spaces, like their previous exhibitions at the UNESCO World Heritage Site Nijo Castle, also located in Kyoto. Through their project Naked Garden One Kyoto, they aim to connect the city’s living heritage with global travelers. As part of this initiative Niwa was created in 2025 on the seventh floor of the East Square in Kyoto Station, featuring dynamic bamboo installations, a tranquil rock garden, and a light-filled modern tearoom named Kiwa.

The new rotating workshops showcase Kyoto’s traditional crafts with practical, artistic activities. You can learn the philosophy of bringing out the natural beauty of flowers through ikebana under the guidance of an instructor from Ikenobo, the founding school of Japanese flower arranging. Textile enthusiasts can try yuzen dyeing by hand-painting handkerchiefs or applying surihaku, which involves stenciling elegant gold and silver leaf onto a tote bag using provided patterns or custom images. Alternatively, you can craft a traditional shikai nami (four-seas wave) bamboo basket to take home, or tackle odoshi, the intricate samurai technique of lacing armor plates together using colorful silk cords.

Joining a session is without challenge for any prospective traveler exploring the city, being located at the city’s gateway and main transportation hub. Workshops are held every Tuesday and Thursday between 2:00 p.m. and 5:00 p.m., lasting roughly 40 to 60 minutes per experience. At 4,500 yen (US$28) per person, each ticket includes a complimentary matcha latte or coffee from the Niwa cafe.

Classes hold up to six people (participation is available from just one person), require zero preparation, and offer clear English text guides alongside instruction in Japanese. It is possible to reserve spots online via KKday or Asoview, or simply walk in for same-day booking up until 4:00 p.m.. Whether you have a spare hour before catching the train to your next destination or want to kick off your Kyoto stay with some real artisan crafts, Niwa offers an easily accessible opportunity to learn a skill and walk away with a unique Japanese souvenir.

title: Japan’s Tsukimi One-hand Bento’s name is all wrong, but it still looks entirely delicious
description: Name could have used some more time in the kitchen, but we still want these in our stomach ASAP. Today we’re talking about some hearty fare, and it comes with an extra-large portion of linguistics to chew on, so let’s dig in. One-hand Bento by Hokkahokka-tei is a relatively new spinoff from Japan’s chain of […]
content:
Name could have used some more time in the kitchen, but we still want these in our stomach ASAP.

Today we’re talking about some hearty fare, and it comes with an extra-large portion of linguistics to chew on, so let’s dig in.

One-hand Bento by Hokkahokka-tei is a relatively new spinoff from Japan’s chain of Hokkahokka-tei takeout shops that specialize in bento, or boxed lunches. Hokkahokka-tei is a national chain, but they’re headquartered in Osaka, so they had a presence at the Expo 2025 world’s fair that took place in the city, where they offered something they called the “one-hand bento,” a heaping helping of rice, vegetables, and meat, folded over so that you can hold the contents of a bento in one hand.

The one-hand bento proved to be a hit at Expo 2025, so after the event ended, the decision was made to open a permanent One-hand Bento by Hokkahokka-tei　shop inside Osaka entertainment complex Abeno Harukas. That happened back in April of this year, meaning the shop is heading into its first autumn, and so also its first tsukimi (moon-viewing) season.

In its culinary sense, tsukimi got its start with noodles, with the term referring to cracking a raw egg into the broth. From there, we’ve seen tsukimi applied to burgers featuring a fried egg, plus pizzas and sandwiches with soft-boiled eggs. That brings us to One-hand Bento by Hokkahokka-tei’s debut tsukimi creations, the debatably named One-hand Bento Tsukimi Wagyu and One-hand Bento Tsukimi Chicken.

The Tsukimi Wagyu One-hand Bento makes use of Naniwa kurogyu, a type of wagyu beef raised in Osaka Prefecture, prepared by simmering in a sweet and savory sukiyaki broth. As you can see, it also has a boiled egg. Well, half a boiled egg, technically, but the linguistic issue is that it doesn’t really look much like a moon.

With the original tsukimi noodles, fried-egg tsukimi burgers, or soft-boiled egg pizzas and sandwiches, the eggs all have a circular shape resembling the full moon, and since Japanese moon-viewing parties are traditionally held on full-moon nights, that’s why the “tsukimi” name started being given to foods. On the other hand, the moon never really looks like a half-sliced boiled egg, and even if it did, those wouldn’t be the nights on which moon-viewing is going on.

There’s a similar situation with the One-hand Bento Tsukimi Chicken (which, like the wagyu version, is priced at 756 yen [US$4.75]). Instead of wagyu beef you get teriyaki chicken, accented with a touch of spicy mayo, and sliced grilled eggplant. Once again, though, the supposed “tsukimi” qualification comes from half a boiled egg.

While we’re on the subject on linguistics, let’s take a look at the other parts of the Tsukimi One-hand Bento name. Yes, it’s true that bento contain both rice and other items, but so too do rice balls, called either onigiri or musubi in Japanese. Sure, these are some very big rice balls, with a much greater variety of fillings than the one or maybe two items you’ll find in most typical onigiri, but since they’re completely lacking a container, it’s hard to argue that they should be called bento, i.e. boxed lunches.

And as for being “one-hand,” sure, they may be big enough that you’ll need to be careful balancing them, but size-wise, you can fit them on your palm…but take a second and think about what would happen if you tried to eat them with just one hand.

Close your fingers around it, and you’re going to be squeezing directly into the topping. Even with a non-tsukimi One-hand Bento, like the one pictured above, you’re going to be digging your digits into something meaty, and with the new tsukimi versions, you’ll be squishing down into the yolk of the egg. So odds are you’re going to need to use two hands to eat these things, either so that you can pluck the topping off and eat it by itself first before you move on to the rest of it, or to stabilize the stack as you peck like a bird to get the topping items in your mouth.

With all of that said, though, you can’t literally eat words, and while their names may be wonky, that doesn’t at all change the fact that the Tsukimi One-hand Bento look delicious, and would make for infinitely better meal choices than something with air-tight naming but questionable flavor. So while they may not really be tsukimi, bento, or one-hand, they’re sure to be popular and are on sale now.

title: Starbucks Japan releases new coffee table book featuring 18 of the most unique stores around the country
description: Photo book takes you on a journey through some of the most iconic Starbucks stores in Japan. content:
Photo book takes you on a journey through some of the most iconic Starbucks stores in Japan.

Japan is home to some of the most beautiful and distinctive Starbucks stores in the world, and now there’s an easy way to explore their unique design features, through a special photo book called Starbucks Coffee Japan Store Design Works 002.

This new book follows on from the success of the 001 volume, released in 2025, which features 17 stores that opened or underwent renovations between 2023 and 2024. The 002 issue expands on this concept, shining a spotlight on 18 stores that opened or were renovated between autumn 2024 and spring 2026.

Designed as a coffee table book, the 002 version dives deeper into the store designs and the local stories behind the cafes, creating a substantial volume that has more pages than the first.

Some of the stores featured in the new book include:

The Cafe & Art Gallery Yanaka Gotenzaka branch in Tokyo, which recently opened as a space that combines coffee with contemporary art by emerging local artists.

The Yoshinogari Historical Park store in Saga, which is located inside an important archaeological site that encompasses a large ancient settlement from the Yayoi Period (300 BC to 300 AD), and the Miyakonojo Kirishima Greenship store in Miyazaki, which was created through a joint project with Kirishima Shuzo, a local distillery founded in 1916.

▼ The Miyakonojo Kirishima store, as it looked during the design phase.

Other Starbucks locations include Ginza House, Cafe & Art Gallery Kyoto BAL, Hokkaido Ballpark F Village, Tokyo Skytree Town, Kyoto Maruyama Park and several stores in Okinawa. Starbucks Reserve cafes and locations inside shopping centres and service areas also feature in the book.

▼ The recently opened Shibuya Tsutaya branch appears in the book as well.

The beautiful photos help to capture the unique feel of each store, while also giving us a sense of the wider culture that exists in the local environment around them.

▼ The 144-page book comes in a beautiful craft paper envelope for gift-giving.

The stores that appear in the book are just a drop in the ocean for the green mermaid’s approximately 2,100 Starbucks stores across Japan, giving us a tantalising taste of what’s out there beyond our local store.

It makes for a great souvenir and keepsake from your time in Japan, and it can be purchased at Starbucks Japan’s online store for 4,800 yen (US$30).

title: New Japanese convenience store rice balls taste like instant noodles [Taste test]
description: Nissin’s Donbei comes to Family Mart in a new form. On our most recent visit to Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart, we walked right over to the shelf where they keep the rice balls. The usual range of fillings and flavors, such as salmon and tuna, were all there, but the one we picked […]
content:
Nissin’s Donbei comes to Family Mart in a new form.

On our most recent visit to Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart, we walked right over to the shelf where they keep the rice balls. The usual range of fillings and flavors, such as salmon and tuna, were all there, but the one we picked out was a noodle-flavored rice ball.

▼ This one

OK, we should probably clarify that. Family Mart is currently celebrating the 45th anniversary of the chain’s founding, and it’s marking the occasion by partnering up with a number of popular snack and other food brands for special crossover items. One of those partners is Nissin, makers of some of Japan’s favorite instant noodles, including Donbei, an instant udon in the “kitsune” style, which means it comes with a slice of fried tofu…so the Dongitsune Musubi rice ball comes with one too.

At a glance, this might look like inarizushi, a traditional Japanese food that’s made by wrapping vinegared rice inside of fried tofu, but there are some key differences that set it apart and connect it to Donbei udon instead. For starters, there’s no vinegar used, and the rice is flavored with the same dashi soup stock used for Nissin’s udon broth.

On top of that, or inside the rice, to be more precise, there are pieces of kamaboko (fish sausage). Kamaboko is also a topping that comes with Donbei, and while it’s sliced into discs when used as an udon topping, here it’s chopped into cubes, adding some stimulating texture variation to the rice ball.

All of these little details come together beautifully as you take a bite. The fried tofu is extremely juicy without being soggy, providing a sweetly refreshing element. The rice, meanwhile, is immensely flavorful and satisfying. This isn’t rice with a suggestion of udon broth flavor added as an open-secret nod to its inspiration. It tastes just like the type of dashi used in Donbei, and if you’re a fan of Nissin’s noodles (like Final Fantasy VII’s Sephiroth is), you’ll probably fall in love with this right away too.

▼ Donbei in its original instant udon form

Ah, but if you’re already a Donbei connoisseur, you might be asking if Family Mart’s rice ball tastes like the Donbei sold at stores in east Japan or west Japan. After all, Nissin uses two slightly different recipes for the noodles’ broth, catering to east Japan’s preference for more boldly flavorful dashi, and west Japan’s fondness for a more subtle taste. The answer is that the Donbei rice balls taste like both: the ones sold at Family Marts in east Japan recreate the flavor of east-Japan Donbei, and Family Marts in west Japan have rice balls that taste like west-Japan Donbei.

▼ If you’re not sure which yours is, you can check the wrapper for the kanji character for east (東) or west (西).

The Dongitsune Musubi is priced at 248 yen (US$1.60), is on sale at Family Mart now, and will be available for a limited time.

content:
Anime characters with beautiful details will keep you smiling all year long. 

One of the things we love about Studio Ghibli is how it likes to share its success by collaborating with local companies, bringing them to the plate so they can share the spotlight together. Noritake is one such company, drawing on its 120-plus years of history and expertise to produce ceramics for the studio, with the limited-edition “Yearly Plate” being an annual tradition that fans look forward to.

Though the design changes every year, My Neighbour Totoro is always the star, and for 2027 we have some familiar characters greeting us from amongst the floral forest setting.

Up top, we have the Catbus, beautifully rendered in watercolour and complete with mouse lights and a destination marker that reads “うち” (“home“). Look closely and you’ll spot Mei and Satsuki enjoying the ride from inside, and galloping up the rear is a surprise appearance by the Kittenbus, distinguished by its yet-to-grow teeth.

On the left is Totoro, perched on a camphor leaf and holding a beautiful evening primrose in his hand, with a smile to bring happiness to your days.

▼ On the right, you’ll find the blue Medium Totoro, carrying its iconic sack of acorns.

▼ And at the bottom sits the white Small Totoro, peering out from a log that reads “2027“.

Soot Sprites, butterflies and wildflowers like valerian, carnations, and bellflowers add countryside charm to the design on both the front and back of the plate.

▼ The plate comes with a wooden stand and is beautifully packaged in a special box, making it ideal for gift-giving.

With soft, delicate touches and meticulous attention to detail, this is a plate that will put a smile on your face all year long. It’ll also be highly sought after, because like last year’s offering, it’ll only be available while stocks last, and if the product sells out after pre-sales begin at 12:00 p.m. on 5 September, it won’t be provided for general sale.

So if you’d like to purchase the Yearly Plate, it’s best to grab it online here through the pre-sale, with deliveries scheduled for mid-to-late November.

title: New Pokémon anniversary song is 22 minutes long, features all 1,025 Pokémon species [Video]
description: Because every Pokémon is somebody’s all-star. There have been a lot of special events and surprises this year celebrating Pokémon’s 30th anniversary, and the latest one is a new song from singer Masayoshi Oishi. Of course, even if this is a way of singing happy birthday to the Pocket Monsters, some of them are going […]
content:
Because every Pokémon is somebody’s all-star.

There have been a lot of special events and surprises this year celebrating Pokémon’s 30th anniversary, and the latest one is a new song from singer Masayoshi Oishi. Of course, even if this is a way of singing happy birthday to the Pocket Monsters, some of them are going to have be left out of the lyrics, right?

Nope. “Pokémon All-stars 1,025” is, as the title implies, a song about all 1,025 Pokémon that have appeared in the series so far, and each and every one of them gets a shout-out in the song. And if you’re thinking there’s no way to condense all that done to the four minutes or so the average anime or video game theme song runs, you’re absolutely right, as the song clocks in at 22 minutes in length.

In addition to having its name soulfully sung by Oishi, each Pokémon also gets a scrapbook collage. These aren’t CG, either, as each was made by hand, combining images from across Pokémon video games, anime, card games, and merch.

▼ There’s also a visit to Japan’s Poképark Kanto Pokémon theme park at the video’s 18:12 mark.

Because of how long the song is, it switches musical styles a few times, incorporating pop, rock, jazz, bossa nova, operatic, and even traditional Japanese instrumental influences. The variations help keep the song from getting repetitive, even with its incredible length, and the species alternate between being grouped by Type, evolution family, or rhyming names.

Speaking of which. the song uses the Japanese versions of the species’ names, so, for example, you’ll hear Oishi sing Fushigidane (a pun on the Japanese phrase Fushigi da ne, “Mysterious, isn’t it?”, and tane/dane, meaning “seed”) instead of Bulbasaur, and Casey instead of Abra. In that sense, it doubles as a vocabulary primer for talking about the series in Japanese.

But there’s more to the lyrics than just a run through the Pokédex page titles. There’s a recurring chorus, which Oishi says he really put his whole heart into, as he sings

That’s right, you’re all stars! There are no bit players here!

Oishi says it was important to him to validate all 1,025 Pokémon. After all, the bond between fans and their favorite is often based on something deeper than simple in-game stats or metagame viability.

If you want to sing along with that part, the lyrics are:

Saa, minna ga shuyaku da
Wakiyaki wa doko ni mo inai

Oishi likens the recording process to running a marathon, and says he started crying when he finished. You can hear his voice crack with emotion as he calls out the name of the 1,025th Pokémon in the lyrics, Mew.

“Maybe someday I’ll go back and do a cleaner-sounding rerecording,” mused Oishi, but it’s hard to imagine improving on the emotional journey the song takes listeners on. If Oishi does step back into the recording booth, hopefully it won’t be for a redo, but a sequel, as the video ends with the sound of an ocean breeze…

…and three blank pages waiting for their collages to be made, a clear nod to the upcoming Pokémon Winds and Waves games.

title: Lego PlayStation recreates Sony’s original console, makes unusual choice for games to salute
description: Lego version of the launch PS1 reproduces the style and size of the landmark piece of game-changing video game tech. When the original PlayStation launched back in December of 1994, it was an odd-looking design. CD-based gaming was still something new for many mass-market console gamers, making the clamshell-lid design an unfamiliar element, and the […]
content:
Lego version of the launch PS1 reproduces the style and size of the landmark piece of game-changing video game tech.

When the original PlayStation launched back in December of 1994, it was an odd-looking design. CD-based gaming was still something new for many mass-market console gamers, making the clamshell-lid design an unfamiliar element, and the controller seemed downright bizarre, with its two-pronged form and lack of exposed center for the directional pad.

It wouldn’t become long, though, until the PlayStation’s mix of high-tech edges, inviting curves, and playful splashes of color became something gamers became very accustomed to, the visual prelude to the fun of playing the lion’s share of memorable blockbusters and niche titles of the 32-bit era. In recognition of the PlayStation’s now iconic design, it’s about to become the latest piece of video game retro tech to inspire its own Lego set.

The straightforwardly named Lego PlayStation recreates what you got in the PlayStation box on launch day: the console itself and one controller (Sony’s tradition of naming its controllers “Dual-something” didn’t start until later in the PlayStation’s life with the introduction its analog controllers in 1997). And yes, it includes the cord, so that you can plus it into the console.

The console’s buttons for opening the lid and turning on the power can be pushed and are functional. Look closely, and you’ll see that Lego has left a slit in front of the power button, where the PlayStation’s green power indicator light would glow when the system was turned on, and it seems like that effect will be reproduced, judging from the preview announcement in which Lego’s design director says “We have the opening button, we have the light.”

The Lego PlayStation is a 1,911-piece set. If you’re a master builder and thinking that number seems too high for what’s seen in the above photos, your keen eyes aren’t deceiving you, because in addition to the console and controller, the kit includes parts to build diorama-like scenes of Gran Turismo and Ape Escape, two of Sony’s biggest first-party hits from the PS1 days.

The scenes can be displayed separately from the console, or they can be slid inside it so that they occupy the area underneath the lid.

It is, admittedly, a little odd that, despite the set recreating the system’s original controller, the two games being given a physical shout-out are both titles that were heavily promoted in conjunction with the PlayStation’s analog controller, which wouldn’t come out until a few years later. As a matter of fact, Ape Escape was the first PlayStation game that required an analog controller, meaning that it couldn’t actually be played with the controller recreated in the Lego set.

▼ Try not to let that upset you too much, though, and instead choose to be upset that Ape Escape wasn’t released worldwide under its Japanese title, Saru Get You.

Lego says the console “Measures over 2.5 inches. (6 centimeters) high, 10.5 inches. (26 centimeters) wide and 7.5 inches (19 centimeters) deep.” Setting aside the unusual vagueness of the “over” part, that would make the Lego PlayStation pretty much the same size as the actual system was.

Regional pricing for the set will be 27,980 yen in Japan, US$179.99 in the U.S., 139,99 pounds in the U.K., and 159.99 Euros in the EU. Preorders open through the respective Lego online shops on October 1 for Lego Insiders with Early Access privileges, and October 4 for everyone else.

title: Movie about Shinzo Abe assassination reportedly in the works
description: Too soon? In 2022, former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who at the time had retired and was a Member of Parliament, was shot on the street while campaigning for a fellow party member in Nara City and died soon after. It was a shocking incident in a country with very strict gun control, which the […]
content:
Too soon?

In 2022, former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who at the time had retired and was a Member of Parliament, was shot on the street while campaigning for a fellow party member in Nara City and died soon after. It was a shocking incident in a country with very strict gun control, which the killer, Tetsuya Yamagami, circumvented by building a gun from pipes and a wooden board.

The case took an even more surreal turn in the aftermath of the incident, when it was learned that Yamagami had intended to kill Abe partly because of his connection with the Unification Church, which he claimed bankrupted his mother years earlier. As a result, connections between the religion and Japanese government were heavily scrutinized, and in 2026, the Unification Church was stripped of its official religious status in Japan. It’s something that’s only happened to two other groups before, one of which was Aum Shinrikyo, whose members carried out a sarin gas attack on the Tokyo subway system.

The entire case became a murky chapter in Japanese history, but it appears a movie based on the events that transpired is in the works by an unnamed studio and director, both of whom are said to be well-known in Japan. One name that has been mentioned by an unnamed source is actor and singer Masaki Suda, but his agency has not commented on the matter.

▼ Suda made his debut in Kamen Rider W (he’s the guy seen below without a hat), and was the youngest actor to ever play a Kamen Rider, at 16 years old, though I suppose he was technically only half of a Kamen Rider.

According to insiders who spoke with Tokyo Sports, the movie will be from the perspective of reporters covering the incident, possibly to minimize the chances of appearing biased in this potentially politically charged subject matter. However, the insider also said that producers are expecting the controversy surrounding the film to make it one of the highest-grossing of all time in Japan.

Comments online seem almost unanimously against this movie being made, with the biggest point of debate being whether this is bad because it promotes terrorism or bad because there isn’t enough substance to warrant making a decent movie about it.

“Is there really a need to turn this into a movie?”
“Who’s going to play Abe?”
“This is abnormal and bizarre… There are still people living through this, and the trial isn’t even concluded yet.”
“Does this guy even have enough backstory for a movie?”
“It makes me sick that they’re turning Prime Minister Abe’s assassination into entertainment.”
“Unbelievable. Surely they’re not going to glorify a terrorist like Yamagami.”
“I don’t think we should be giving this person any more attention.”
“This is probably going to backfire on them. Who wants to see a movie about this anyway?”
“Is a movie about an incident caused by the whim of some idiot who hated his life and blamed everyone else really going to be interesting?”
“I hope this is just a hoax. This movie shouldn’t be made.”

It could be said that this is a knee-jerk reaction to the news, and over time, morbid curiosity will bring people to the theaters if this movie is ever released. Then again, within days of the killing, a rough cut of another film, Revolution+1, was screened by former Japanese Red Army member and director Masao Adachi on the date of Abe’s state funeral.

The film follows the story of a man named Tatsuya Kawakami, but mirrors the reported life of Tetsuya Yamagami very closely. It was a low-budget independent movie with a limited screening, and ultimately still hasn’t generated a great deal of attention from the public at large.

So it’s a long shot that an Abe assassination dramatization, only a few years after the incident occurred, would be boffo box-office. There’s been a great deal of secrecy surrounding the project, so only time will tell if they even go through with it from here on out.

title: Japanese Starbucks that’s also an art gallery hosts exhibition by painters from Tokyo’s top art school
description: Starbucks in artsy neighborhood wants to showcase work by local creatives. There are a lot of Starbucks dotting the map of Tokyo, but only one of them is also an art gallery. Back in March, Starbucks Japan opened a new branch in the city’s Yanaka neighborhood, known as an enclave for artists and other creative […]
content:
Starbucks in artsy neighborhood wants to showcase work by local creatives.

There are a lot of Starbucks dotting the map of Tokyo, but only one of them is also an art gallery. Back in March, Starbucks Japan opened a new branch in the city’s Yanaka neighborhood, known as an enclave for artists and other creative types, and in addition to an especially stylish interior, the coffeehouse also has ample space for displaying works of art.

Like any proper art facility, Starbucks Cafe and Art Gallery Yanaka Godenzaka, as the branch is called, periodically cycles in new pieces to display, and as of September 4 it’s started its third exhibition since its opening. This one is extra special, since it’s a joint project with Tokyo University of the Arts. The public university, also known as Tokyo Geidai, is considered to be one of the finest art schools in the country, and its main campus in Ueno Park is just a 15-minute walk from the Starbucks gallery.

So while they may not be literal neighbors, Starbucks still wants to extend a neighborly sentiment by serving as the venue for an exhibition by eight students in Tokyo University of the Arts’s Department of Oil Painting 6th Laboratory creative unit. The event, titled GABE6‒Drawing as Practice, is described as “focusing on drawing as an aspect of the daily creative process” and invites guests to “enjoy the diverse artistic expression born of the exhibiting artists’ individual thoughts and inquisitiveness.”

The exhibition (which has no admission fee beyond the price of your Starbucks order) opened on September 4, the same day as this year’s iteration of Tokyo University of the Arts’ annual Geidai campus festival, so visiting both on the same extra-cultured day is an option. However, while Geidai only runs until September 9, GABE6‒Drawing as Practice will continue on through October 12, giving the student artists an opportunity to share their creations and possibly turn some coffee fans into art fans as well.

title: Kyoto temple bans visitors from wearing kimono
description: Visitors to 600-year-old temple prohibited from wearing traditional garment following problems caused by those prioritizing cool social media photos over basic manners. Seiraiin is a temple in Kyoto’s Gion district, founded some 600 years ago and known for its beautiful garden and dynamic white dragon painting on the ceiling of its main hall. Ordinarily, its […]
content:
Visitors to 600-year-old temple prohibited from wearing traditional garment following problems caused by those prioritizing cool social media photos over basic manners.

Seiraiin is a temple in Kyoto’s Gion district, founded some 600 years ago and known for its beautiful garden and dynamic white dragon painting on the ceiling of its main hall. Ordinarily, its traditional aesthetics would make it a perfect place to visit on a day of sightseeing while dressed in a kimono.

However, Seiraiin recently announced that would-be visitors wearing kimono are prohibited from entering the temple grounds.

▼ Seiraiin’s white dragon painting, which visitors are encouraged to view by lying on the tatami reed flooring and looking up at it

View this post on Instagram

The reason for the unexpected policy, announced in July, is one that’s becoming all too common in Kyoto: bad-mannered tourists. The temple says that it has been experiencing problems with people coming to take elaborate and invasive photos on the temple grounds. In addition to making it difficult for other visitors to use the temple’s facilities as intended (as a place to offer prayers and appreciate its art), the temple says there have been multiple instances of visitors entering restricted areas and causing damage to the temple while posing for photos, such as stepping into a raked rock garden or opening up a sliding door without permission and damaging it in the process.

None of the damage was caused as a direct result of wearing kimono, and the temple has said that its complaint is not with the practice itself of wearing the garment. However, the proportion of problematic photo-takers who wear kimono is large enough that the temple has apparently concluded that banning such attire is a necessary precaution against visitors for feel the importance of getting a cool photo of themselves to post on social media trumps being polite or preserving a cultural site.

In addition to kimono, Seiraiin also established a rule prohibiting the wearing of “Japanese-style clothing” and “costumes.” This doesn’t appear to have been a snap decision, either. Seiraiin is one of a number of sub-temples located within the perimeter of Kenninji Temple, which itself posted a statement on its website in November of last year reminding visitors that “Our temple is not a photo studio, theme park, or similar facility,” and that visitors displaying impolite or inappropriate behavior will be asked to leave.

The situation ties into many different points about Japanese cultural traditions and their places in modern society. To start with, Japan has no taboos against non-Japanese people wearing kimono, and most locals are happy to see foreigners taking a participatory interest in the country’s customs. It’s also largely understood and accepted that those with an interest in classical Japanese fashion often enjoy other traditional aesthetics as well, which is why kimono rental shops are often found in cities and neighborhoods with historic quarters, such as Kyoto. And while Japan’s temples are, of course, religious institutions, even many Japanese visitors are drawn to them for their picturesque qualities or historic significance more than out of spiritual fervor. Many temples embrace the photogenic nature of their appeal, including Seiraiin, which has spaces where visitors can enjoy refreshments while looking out over its garden.

View this post on Instagram

However, if there’s one rule that supersedes all others in Japanese culture, it’s to be considerate of others, and it’s a clear violation of that to treat a temple like it’s your private rented-out photo spot.

Seiraiin appears to be the only temple so far to have instituted a no-kimono rule, but with overtourism being something on the mind of just about every noteworthy destination in Kyoto, no doubt others are watching to see the results. Hopefully, if and when the situation improves, Seiraiin will feel comfortable walking back the restriction, but for now, this is a reminder for all travelers to avoid acting like selfish jerks and ruining things for everyone else.

title: Starbucks Japan adds new Sweet Potato Frappuccino and Latte to the menu, but do they deliver the taste of autumn?
description: New drinks coincide with the opening of the chain’s new “Customisation Bar”, giving us a hack for making them even better.   There’s now a distinct feeling of autumn in the air, and Starbucks is heralding its arrival in Japan with a very distinctive autumnal flavour: sweet potato. The ingredient is being showcased in two […]
content:
New drinks coincide with the opening of the chain’s new “Customisation Bar”, giving us a hack for making them even better.  

There’s now a distinct feeling of autumn in the air, and Starbucks is heralding its arrival in Japan with a very distinctive autumnal flavour: sweet potato. The ingredient is being showcased in two new drinks, the Torori Mitsuimo Beni Haruka Frappuccino and the Torori Mitsuimo Beni Haruka Mousse Tea Latte, which went on sale on 2 September.

With “torori” meaning “melty” or “gooey”, and “mitsuimo” (“honey potato”) referring to its thick sweetness, the Japanese names sound enticing to the ear, but would they be just as enticing to the palate? That was something our resident Starbucks expert, K. Masami, was keen to find out, so she lined up early when the drinks were released, and purchased them both for a tasting.

▼ She started the proceedings with the Tea Latte, which is sold in Small through to Venti sizes, from 640 yen (US$4.35).

The beauty of this drink lies in its many layers – take a preliminary sip and you’ll get a beautiful mouthful of honey-like sweetness from the chilled sweet potato paste in the base. Move the straw up slightly, and you’ll be able to enjoy a layer filled with milk tea, made with Darjeeling and Assam for a bold yet aromatic and refreshing astringency, before finishing with the fluffy mouthfeel of the sweet-potato-flavoured mousse topping.

As the drink contains a pre-blended tea mix, it can’t be customised with a different type of milk, so that’s something you might need to be aware of, but thankfully for Masami, that wasn’t a concern. After enjoying the layers separately she mixed them all together, and that’s when the beverage levelled up, taking on a richer, deeper flavour and consistency, and making every sip taste like Japanese autumn.

Masami loved the way Starbucks chose to use the Beni Haruka sweet potato variety, as it’s the one that’s most ubiquitous in Japan so it delivered all the familiar, nostalgic flavours from way back in her childhood. It worked a treat in the Frappuccino too, proudly showing off its sweet, rich flavour with the addition of crispy roasted sweet potato-flavoured pieces on top. These pieces are inspired by “imomitsu” (“potato honey”), which is the caramelised, honey-like juices that ooze out and harden on the surface of a sweet potato as it bakes, and they added an extra layer of authentic flavour to every mouthful.

▼ Frappuccino on the left

Another surprise awaiting customers from 2 September is the new “Customisation Bar”, which lets customers add various extras to their drinks, to personalise the flavours.

▼ The five optional add-ons are: Vanilla Sugar & Salt, Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce, Ginger Sugar Chips, and Cinnamon Powder and Honey.

Masami had requested almond milk for her Frappuccino (the milk in the Frappuccino can be customised) so as she walked by the customisation bar, she couldn’t resist adding a sprinkling of cinnamon, which she thought might pair well with the slightly nutty flavour.

Taking a sip with the cinnamon made her fall even deeper in love with the Frappuccino, as it paired exceptionally well with the sweet potato. As a lover of spice, she would even go as far as to say that the drink felt complete after the cinnamon had been added, and she ended up wishing she’d tried it on the latte too.

There’s something about cinnamon that really helps to being things to life in a very autumnal way, so if you do get to order one of these drinks, she highly recommends adding it if you can. It’ll really get you in the mood for all things autumn, and with a very distinctive seasonal ingredient as the main star, the flavour of Japanese autumn will stay with you as a fond memory after the very last sip.

title: Solo travel in Japan: $3 all-you-can-drink deal at this conveyor belt restaurant is a fun time for one
description: No need to feel self-conscious when you can use this automatic ordering and delivery system. Drinking in Tokyo on your own might sound like a daunting prospect for solo travellers in Japan, but if you know where to go it can be a fun time to remember, especially when it doesn’t break the bank. Our […]
content:
No need to feel self-conscious when you can use this automatic ordering and delivery system.

Drinking in Tokyo on your own might sound like a daunting prospect for solo travellers in Japan, but if you know where to go it can be a fun time to remember, especially when it doesn’t break the bank.

Our team of reporters are seasoned solo dining pros, always on the lookout for new places to eat and drink on their own, and their most recent find is one of the cheapest deals in town, letting you drink as much as you like for 90 minutes for the one-coin price of 500 yen (US$3.13).

The so-called “One-Coin All-You-Can-Drink” campaign comes from Yakiniku no Watami, a yakiniku chain that’s been taking over locations that formerly belonged to the now-phased-out Watami izakaya chain.

Our reporter Ahiruneko discovered the deal and immediately set out to try it, and when he arrived at his nearest branch shortly after midday, he was shown to a table seat as the solo seats at the counter were already full.

Settling into the booth, Ahiruneko was impressed by the setup – food is delivered via a “Special Express Lane” beside the table, and orders are made using a touchscreen panel.

▼ Like conveyor belt sushi, only with meat and alcohol.

Ahiruneko was here for the “One-Coin All-You-Can-Drink” deal, and sure enough it was being advertised with a laminated flyer at the table, which details of the 18 types of alcohol you can order over 90 minutes.

▼ Highballs, Sours, Gins and Mixers.

Bracing himself for the fine print, he looked closely at the details and was impressed again. Ahiruneko had assumed there would be restrictions like a table charge, an appetiser charge, or a requirement for at least two dishes per person, but the only real condition was ordering at least 500 yen worth of food, which was totally fine as he wouldn’t want to drink on an empty stomach anyway.

This is the full list of fine-print details:

・You need to order at least 500 yen worth of food (including tax)
・You can combine it with either an all-you-can-eat plan or individual dishes
・It can be ordered during either lunch or dinner hours
・You can also use the soft drink bar
・Last orders are 15 minutes before the 90-minute mark
・Draft beer is not included

You don’t often come across an all-you-can-drink deal with such easy requirements, so Ahiruneko wasted no time in ordering the “Watami Kalbi Lunch” for 1,089 yen, as the accompaniment for his day drinking.

When ordering his all-you-can-drink option, he found that he had to call a member of staff over first, as they needed to set up the touchscreen panel for the all-you-can-drink menu to appear.

▼ Highballs, lemon sours, tea-based drinks and Suntory Sui gin soda are some of the included options.

He made his selections and then, after waiting a little while…

▼ … his lunch and highball arrived on the lane.

The sight of his meal arriving, like a train pulling into a station, added a fantastic touch of excitement to his solo meal. Plucking his meal tray off the delivery tray, he saw that the Watami Kalbi was thicker than expected, making him one happy diner.

Giving it a light grill, Ahiruneko was very pleased with how his meal was turning out, and things got even better when he took a sip of his drink.

▼ Ahhhh, that hits the spot.

It didn’t take long for Ahiruneko to polish off his drink along with delicious bites of succulent meat, so he immediately ordered another beverage, and…

▼ … it arrived on the express lane.

This all-you-can-drink delivery system is one you don’t encounter very often, and it was Ahiruneko’s first time seeing it. Usually, even if you order by touchscreen, staff deliver drinks to your table, and as someone who feels slightly awkward with staff interactions, this system was ideal.

▼ In fact,  it was so ideal that he ended up downing seven drinks in 90 minutes.

Doing the math, that works out to about 71 yen ($0.46) per drink, which is pretty mind-blowing. Even when he factored in the meal cost, which brought the total to 1,589 yen, it was still a great deal that he would definitely go back for.

So in the end, Ahiruneko left the restaurant with a heavier belly, a lighter mood, and only a slightly lighter wallet. The one downside to the deal is it’s only available for a limited time until 17 September, and at limited locations, which we’ve listed for you below.

Participating Restaurants

Tokyo: Otorii Station Front, Kinshicho South Exit Station Front, Kokubunji South Exit, Chofu South Exit, Shimura-Sakaue, Ikebukuro East Exit, Kameari Station Front
Saitama: Kawagoe East Exit Crea Mall, Asakadai Station Front
Kanagawa: Yokohama
Aichi: Meieki, Higashi-Okazaki Station Front, Motoyama Station Front
Osaka: Namba, Umeda Chayamachi
Hyogo: Kawanishi-Noseguchi Station Front, Akashi Station Front, Ono
Nara: Yamato-Yagi South Exit

title: American tourist in Japan arrested on charges of attempted murder and arson
description: Arrest follows Okinawan hotel fire that took place last month. Okinawa offers a wide range of activities for travelers to enjoy. content:
Arrest follows Okinawan hotel fire that took place last month.

Okinawa offers a wide range of activities for travelers to enjoy. It boasts Japan’s finest beaches, perfect for relaxing or marine sports such as snorkeling and scuba diving. The prefecture’s dense jungles offer ample hiking opportunities, and its unique Ryukyu cultural heritage can be experienced both at historical sites such as Shuri Castle and through the many restaurants serving traditional Okinawan cuisine.

Generally not recommended for visitors though? Arson and attempted murder, the activities for which one American tourist has been arrested on charges of.

In the pre-dawn hours of August 15, a fire broke out at Hamby Resort in the Chatan neighborhood of Okinawa City. The hotel, located a few blocks from both the shoreline and United States Marine Corps Camp Foster, had 19 guests staying in its trailer-style bungalows, close to full capacity during the busy Obon vacation period.

▼ Video of the fire

Thankfully, no lives were lost, although one guest, a 55-year-old man from Osaka, lost consciousness from smoke inhalation before being rescued by police and U.S. Marine Marshall Martinez, who saw the fire and volunteered to help. The man remains hospitalized in Okinawa.

Six days after the blaze, Posedion Roberson, a 32-year-old American tourist was arrested for trespassing into and sleeping inside a building complex in the town of Urasoe, roughly half an hour south of Chatan. Roberson, it turns out, had also booked a room at the hotel on the night of the fire, but disappeared after the incident, and investigators now believe he was the person responsible. On September 1, he was rearrested on charges of arson and attempted murder, and is currently in police custody.

▼ The hotel, prior to the fire

There’s been a noticeable uptick in high-profile crimes committed by foreign tourists in Japan over the past year or so, including vandalism, assault, and theft. Attempted mass murder, though, is on a whole other level, and if convicted, Roberson is unlikely to receive much in the way of clemency.

title: Mini CRT-lookalike Final Fantasy figurines are awesome pixel art music boxes [Video]
description: Square Enix’s Mini Melody TVs tap into the nostalgia for retro games and old-school electronics. With retro games, there’s often a fine yet indistinct line between games’ whose aesthetics have been canonized as timelessly charming and cultural milestones of digital artistry, and those whose graphics and sounds now merely feel antiquated, making them past their […]
content:
Square Enix’s Mini Melody TVs tap into the nostalgia for retro games and old-school electronics.

With retro games, there’s often a fine yet indistinct line between games’ whose aesthetics have been canonized as timelessly charming and cultural milestones of digital artistry, and those whose graphics and sounds now merely feel antiquated, making them past their expiration date in terms of triggering a warm, fuzzy emotional response. Tapping into gaming nostalgia gets trickier still when you take into account that many fans’ memories aren’t tied only to the games themselves, but to the equipment they were played with, much of which has also now been replaced by newer tech.

So it’s nice to see Square Enix going the extra mile in presenting the Final Fantasy series’ early sights and sounds with these cool, clever figurines that look like CRT television sets.

The Final Fantasy Series–Mini Melody TV collection takes us back to Final Fantasy’s initial pixel art era, consisting of the first six games in the series, which were released for the NES/Famicom and Super NES/Super Famicom. Each figurine’s screen shows a scene from one of the games and also plays an iconic piece of background music from its soundtrack.

For the original Final Fantasy, you’ll see the title screen (which, famously, doesn’t come until after you complete the first objective of our quest) and its rousing musical accompaniment that would go on to become the main theme of Final Fantasy.

Final Fantasy II’s figurine plays “The Rebel Army,” and Final Fantasy III’s “Eternaal Wind.”

The Final Fantasy IV Mini Melody TV shows us Cecil, still in dark knight mode, sailing through the skies to “The Red Wings,” while Final Fantasy V’s recaptures Bartz party’s battle with Gilgamesh, backed by “Battle at the Big Bridge,” a frantic fight theme that’s possibly the most widely remembered thing about the entire game.

And finally, the Final Fantasy VI figurine has us checking in on Setzer, Celes, Edgar, and Sabin aboard the airship Falcon, searching for their lost friends as, fittingly, “Searching for Friends” plays.

Each of the figurines draws power from a AAA battery to light up its screen, which is actually an LCD display, despite the CRT-style casing. With dimensions of 6.2 x 4.45 x 5.3 centimeters (2.4 x 1.3 x 2.1 inches), they’re compact enough to fit more than one on your desk, and you may want to pick up more than one, since they’re being offered as blind-box items, so you won’t know which one you’re getting until after you open it, unless you opt for the complete box set that guaranties you one of each version.

Individual Final Fantasy Series–Mini Melody TVs are priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50) and the complete set at 11,880. They’re scheduled to officially go on sale on January 29.
